docs.title: Views
docs.text:
The dashboard has six views, toggled by tab buttons at the top:

Grading Compliance — lists instructors with counts of overdue ungraded submissions. Clicking a row expands per-course detail; clicking a course opens the full submissions table for that course.

Discussion Response Compliance — lists instructors with their discussion response rates. Response rates are calculated per-discussion topic. Clicking a row expands per-course detail; clicking a course opens the discussion responses table.

Announcements — lists instructors with total announcement counts and scheduled announcement counts per course.

Rubric Compliance — lists instructors with how well they use rubrics when grading: graded submissions on rubric assignments, submissions graded without the rubric, rubric lines graded out of the total (and as a percentage), ungraded lines, rubric line comments, instructor submission comments, and submissions with no feedback at all. Counts are per course, so every active teacher on a course gets that course's totals, and only graded submissions count. Clicking a row expands per-course detail; "View Submissions" opens the per-submission table for that course, where each row links to the submission in SpeedGrader. It uses the same dashboard filter bar and App-level filters (name, term, date range, CE toggle, title list) as the grading view, and the submissions table gets the same filters, so its counts match the row it was opened from. Flags raised from this view are recorded as grading flags, so they show up as grading flags in the Flags view and in the Grading view's flag counts.

Flags — lists all recorded instructor flags (violations). Each row shows flag type (grading, discussions, announcements, other), term, date, and optional reason note. Flags can be edited or deleted inline. Filterable by term, instructor ID, flag type, reason text, and date range.

Grade Distribution — lists per-assignment grade distribution statistics (mean, median, mode, sample standard deviation, min/max percentage and raw scores) aggregated across all sections sharing an assignment template (via master_courses_child_subscriptions). Filterable by term, course code, and assignment title, with an option to group by individual section instead of merging them. Sortable and paginated like the other views, but has no flag column and uses its own term/course-code/title filters instead of the shared dashboard filter bar.

The Grading, Discussion, Announcements and Rubric Compliance views each include a flag column showing the instructor's current-term flag count and total lifetime flag count. Clicking the flag button opens a dialog to record a new flag. They share the same filter controls: instructor name search, date range, term selector, and CE toggle. Picking a term resets the date range to that term's dates, since the grading, discussion, rubric and conversation endpoints reject dates outside the term. "View Submissions" sends the same dates, CE toggle and title filter as the grading counts it was opened from.

Instructor names are rendered as mailto links. Email addresses are derived from the instructor's name (first initial + last name + @unity.edu) because the canvas database does not store email addresses.

Links are set to open in new tab by default (<base target="_blank" />) in index.html

docs.title: State
docs.text:
Each table component owns its filter bar, pagination (usePaginatedTable) and CSV export, and fetches its first page when it mounts. App.tsx holds only what is shared: auth, the view toggle, violation counts, and the dashboard filters (name, term, date range, CE, gallery, title list) used by the grading, discussion, announcement, conversation and rubric tables, so those filters carry over between tabs. Editing a filter shows "Filters changed — click Go to apply"; Go (or Enter in a text filter) fetches page 1 with the new filters, and Prev/Next paginate the current result.

The backend owns the defaults: a table's first fetch sends no sort, term or page size, and the table follows the sort_column/sort_direction/page_size echoed in each response. The CE Only checkbox default, the default excluded assignment titles and the Canvas link prefix come from the backend's /api/config (see src/config.ts), and the current term from /api/current_term, so the frontend .env files only hold hosting paths (VITE_BASE_PATH, VITE_API_BASE). No constants file is shared with the backend.

When a fetch fails, the table keeps its rows and the pagination bar shows the backend's error message (e.g. dates outside the selected term). "Export CSV" fetches every row in the current sort: it asks for them all in one page and then fetches whatever pages the backend's page-size cap left over.

Switching tabs remounts the table, so it refetches. Opening a detail page (submissions, discussion responses, a conversation, rubric submissions) only hides the dashboard, so returning keeps the table's page and sort.

Syncing state is polled every 10 seconds after a manual sync is triggered, and the instructor data is automatically refreshed when the sync completes.

docs.title: Summit
docs.text:
Summit collects game analytics. Use it to find which levels players finish, which steps they repeat, and whether frame rate changes after a release. It can also link a session to its 3D replay in Trailhead.

Start with one synthetic event if you are setting up the service. If you are working on a Unity build, see Connect a Unity game. For dashboard tasks and API entry points, see the data and reporting reference.

docs.title: How an event reaches a report
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Game["Unity game or HTTP client"] -->|Events and performance| Ingest["Summit ingestion API"]
    Game -->|Session lifecycle and feedback| Ingest
    Ingest --> DB[("PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB")]
    Trailhead["Trailhead"] -->|Recording summary| Ingest
    DB --> Dashboard["Summit dashboard and reports"]
    Dashboard -->|Replay link| Trailhead

The API validates game data before writing it to PostgreSQL. TimescaleDB organizes time-series events and performance samples. Dashboard queries use that data for individual sessions and aggregate views.

A player can have multiple sessions. A session can have multiple Trailhead recordings. Summit stores a summary and replay link for each synced recording. Trailhead keeps the frames and events that make up the replay.

docs.title: Source map
docs.text: Area Location Game instrumentation Unity client and API examples Next.js dashboard and API Dashboard source PostgreSQL schema SQL migrations Local setup and branch promotion Project README

docs.title: Data Summit collects
docs.text:
Record What it describes Where to look Session A play interval for an app, with version, player ID, and session metadata Sessions Event A named action with optional properties, measurements, or a numeric value Events Explorer Performance sample Client FPS and memory observations Performance Hardware profile Device information associated with a player across sessions Users Feedback response Answers keyed by the fields of a form or supplied by the game Feedback Trailhead summary A recording ID, metadata, and a replay URL when configured Sessions or Users

An event with an unknown session ID or a session ID from a different app can still appear in Events Explorer. Summit stores that event without a session association. For an integrated replay, the UUID in summit_session_id identifies the Summit session, while the Trailhead recording has its own UUID.

docs.title: Where to answer a question
docs.text: Question View What happened around a specific action? Open the session and inspect its event timeline. Follow its replay link if one is available. At which step do players stop a sequence? Build a funnel from the ordered event names. Does frame rate vary across sessions? Compare FPS in Performance and inspect specific players in Users. What did players report? Filter Feedback and inspect response details and per-question rollups. Which fields recur in a weekly report? Build a custom report from stored fields, save the definition, and export its results as CSV.

docs.title: API entry points
docs.text:
Paths are relative to the application base path. Game ingestion uses the game's app key in x-api-key. Programmatic dashboard queries and app management use the dashboard API key. Browser access uses a signed-in dashboard account.

Operation Route Start or end a session POST /api/ingest/session/start or POST /api/ingest/session/end Record events or samples POST /api/ingest or POST /api/ingest/batch Send device details POST /api/ingest/hardware Load a feedback form or send answers GET /api/feedback/forms or POST /api/ingest/feedback Query recorded events POST /api/query/events Run a custom report definition POST /api/reports/run

See the full API table and the request schemas for route-specific fields.

docs.title: Send your first event
docs.text: Create a disposable app and send an event you can find in Events Explorer. Use the Docker stack so the service runs with the same /summit path as a production build.

docs.title: Start Summit
docs.text:
1. From the repository root, copy .env.example to .env.
  2. Set DB_PASSWORD, DASHBOARD_API_KEY, and SUMMIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env.
  3. Run docker compose up -d.
  4. Open the local dashboard and sign in with the bootstrap administrator account.

On a new stack, PostgreSQL initializes the schema. For database upgrades, follow the migration notes in the repository for the database you are upgrading.

docs.title: Create an app and session
docs.text:
Run these commands from a terminal. Set DASHBOARD_API_KEY in your shell to the value from the local .env file before you begin.

base=http://localhost:8088/summit

curl --fail-with-body -sS "$base/api/apps" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: $DASHBOARD_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"name":"Documentation smoke test"}'

Set APP_API_KEY in your shell to the returned api_key. Run the next request with the app key. The response includes the new session's id.

curl --fail-with-body -sS "$base/api/ingest/session/start" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: $APP_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"user_id":"docs-player","app_version":"0.0.1"}'

docs.title: Track a checkpoint
docs.text:
Set SESSION_ID to the returned id. Send one event to that session.

curl --fail-with-body -sS "$base/api/ingest" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: $APP_API_KEY" \
  --data-binary @- <<JSON
{"events":[{"name":"checkpoint_reached","session_id":"$SESSION_ID","user_id":"docs-player","properties":{"checkpoint":"trail_marker","measurements":{"elapsed_seconds":42}}}]}
JSON

Open the test app in Summit. In Events Explorer, find checkpoint_reached and check the checkpoint and measurement on the event. In Sessions, open the session and find the same event on its timeline.

If the request returns 401, check which key the endpoint expects. If it returns 404, check the base path. A direct Next.js development server serves routes at /api/…, while Docker serves them at /summit/api/….

docs.title: Setting up the Canvas LTI tool
docs.text:
Step by step, from no setup to a student finishing a Storyline course in a Canvas dev course with the score in the gradebook. Production Summit is https://ai2.unity.edu/summit; replace it if you deploy elsewhere. For how the tool works and what it stores, see SCORM courses and Canvas LTI.

Who does what:

Step Who 1 to 3: secrets, deploy, check Whoever runs the Summit deploy (Infisical access) 4: developer key A Canvas admin 5 to 7: client id, install, place a course Summit deployer, then a teacher or designer in the dev course 8: test as a student Anyone with Student View in the dev course

docs.title: 1. Generate the secrets
docs.text:
On any machine with Node 20 and this repository:

cd dashboard
npm run learning:keys
openssl rand -hex 32   # the learning database password

learning:keys prints four values: LEARNING_PSEUDONYM_KEY, LEARNING_VAULT_KEY, LEARNING_TOKEN_SECRET and LTI_TOOL_PRIVATE_KEY. Put them straight into Infisical and don't leave copies elsewhere. Generate them once per environment:

  • A new LEARNING_PSEUDONYM_KEY gives every returning student a new pseudonym, which splits their history.
  • Losing LEARNING_VAULT_KEY means grades can no longer be sent for students already in the database.
  • A new LTI_TOOL_PRIVATE_KEY is picked up by Canvas from /lti/jwks, so it can be rotated, but not mid-launch.

docs.title: 2. Add them to Infisical
docs.text:
Project: the Summit project. Environment: prod. Path: /summit. This is where webhook/deploy_summit.sh reads secrets from before it runs docker compose up -d --build.

Required now:

Secret Value COMPOSE_PROFILES learning. Starts the separate learning database. Without it, the database container doesn't start. LEARNING_DB_PASSWORD The openssl rand -hex 32 value. LEARNING_DATABASE_URL postgresql://summit_learning:<LEARNING_DB_PASSWORD>@summit-learning-db:5432/summit_learning, with the password pasted in. Setting this turns the feature on. LEARNING_PSEUDONYM_KEY From learning:keys. LEARNING_VAULT_KEY From learning:keys. LEARNING_TOKEN_SECRET From learning:keys. LTI_TOOL_PRIVATE_KEY From learning:keys: the whole value between the quotes, on one line with its literal \n escapes. Don't include the quotes. SUMMIT_PUBLIC_URL https://ai2.unity.edu/summit. No trailing slash.

Required after step 4:

Secret Value LTI_CLIENT_ID The Canvas developer key's client id, a long number such as 10000000000123.

Only if they apply:

Secret When Value LTI_PLATFORM_ISSUER Testing on Unity's Canvas test or beta instance instead of production https://canvas.test.instructure.com or https://canvas.beta.instructure.com. Production Canvas, including a dev course in it, needs nothing (default https://canvas.instructure.com). LTI_DEPLOYMENT_IDS To accept launches only from specific installs The deployment id shown when the app is installed, comma-separated. Empty accepts any install of the key. LTI_FRAME_ANCESTORS Canvas is reached on a custom domain rather than *.instructure.com 'self' https://canvas.unity.edu (with the real domain). LEARNING_CAPTURE_FREE_TEXT To keep typed free-text answers (off by default, since they can identify a student) 1 LEARNING_MAX_PACKAGE_MB Course zips over 1 GB A number in MB

Never set in production: LEARNING_DEMO_MODE (lets anyone play courses as made-up learners).

None of these secrets go into git, .env.example or the Canvas developer key. Canvas only ever sees the public half of the tool key, at /lti/jwks.

docs.title: 3. Deploy and check
docs.text:
1. Deploy this branch the usual way (merge to docker, or run the deploy script). The app applies the learning database migrations on start.
  2. If the reverse proxy in front of Summit limits request size, raise it for /summit/api/learning/packages so course zips can be uploaded. For nginx: client_max_body_size 1024m;.
  3. Sign in to Summit as an admin and open Learning, Canvas. Everything under Ready for Canvas? should read Ready except the Canvas developer key, which needs LTI_CLIENT_ID.
  4. Open https://ai2.unity.edu/summit/lti/config and https://ai2.unity.edu/summit/lti/jwks in a browser off the university network (a phone on cellular works). Both must return JSON. Canvas fetches them from the internet.
  5. To let a non-admin account see learning data: Settings, Accounts, Allow learning data.

docs.title: 4. Canvas admin: create the developer key
docs.text:
Send the Canvas admin this:

In Canvas: Admin, the root account, Developer Keys, + Developer Key, + LTI Key.

  • Key name: Summit learning
  • Owner email: the Summit maintainer
  • Redirect URIs: https://ai2.unity.edu/summit/lti/launch
  • Method: Enter URL
  • JSON URL: https://ai2.unity.edu/summit/lti/config

Save, then switch the key On in the State column. Send back the number in the Details column (the client id).

The JSON sets the privacy level to anonymous, so Canvas sends Summit no names or emails. It asks for the Assignment and Grade Services scopes, for line items and scores, so scores can go to the gradebook. Its placements are Assignment Selection and Link Selection.

If Canvas has a test instance and you'd rather start there, create the key in the test instance instead and set LTI_PLATFORM_ISSUER (step 2). Keys don't carry between instances.

docs.title: 5. Add the client id
docs.text:
1. Add LTI_CLIENT_ID to Infisical and redeploy.
  2. On Learning, Canvas, select Check the connection to Canvas. All three checks should pass:
  3. Canvas signing keys: Summit can reach Canvas.
  4. Summit key set, from outside: Summit's public address serves its own key. A warning here only means the server can't reach its own public name; step 3.4 already confirmed Canvas can.
  5. Grade passback token: Canvas accepted Summit's key for this client id. If this fails, the key is off, the client id is wrong, or the key's JWK URL isn't https://ai2.unity.edu/summit/lti/jwks.

docs.title: 6. Install the tool in the dev course
docs.text:
In the dev course: Settings, Apps, View App Configurations, + App. Set Configuration Type to By Client ID, paste the client id and select Submit, then Install.

If the course doesn't allow it, the Canvas admin can install it the same way in the sub-account that holds the dev course.

docs.title: 7. Upload a course and place it
docs.text:
1. Publish from Storyline: Publish, LMS, SCORM 2004 3rd or 4th edition, and zip the output. SCORM 1.2 and xAPI also work.
  2. Upload it: in Summit, Learning, Courses, Upload.
  3. Place it in Canvas: in the dev course, create an Assignment. Set Submission Type to External Tool, select Find, then Summit learning. Summit's course picker opens. Choose the course, select Add to Canvas, then Select. Set the points and Save & Publish.

Summit’s course picker offers a Canvas grading setting for each assignment. Numeric score is the default. Choose Pass/fail to send full credit for an explicit pass and zero for an explicit fail, even when the package reports a separate quiz score. An attempt without a pass/fail outcome stays ungraded. In Canvas, set Display Grade as to Complete/Incomplete and use a positive points value. Summit still records the original score for analytics.

A module item works too (Add item, External Tool, Summit learning), but without an assignment there is no gradebook column, so no score is sent.

docs.title: 8. Test as a student
docs.text:
1. Turn on Student View in the dev course and open the assignment. The course plays inside Canvas.
  2. Go through it and finish the quiz. Leave partway and come back to check resume.
  3. In Summit:
  4. Learning, Canvas: the launch is under Recent launches, and the assignment under Canvas assignments, with a grade sent.
  5. Learning, Overview: select the course to see slides, answers and clicks. The attempt page shows every answer and the timeline.
  6. In Canvas: the Gradebook shows the score for Test Student.

Opening the assignment as a teacher works too, but it's recorded as an instructor try: it gets no grade and is left out of the statistics.

Also try a blueprint sync if the dev course setup has one: place the course in a blueprint, sync it to a child course, and launch from the child. Recent launches shows whether the child came through as its own course and assignment. This shapes how Summit will group dev, blueprint and live courses.

docs.title: When it doesn't work
docs.text:
Learning, Canvas, Recent launches shows each login and launch, which step failed, and why. No user ids are kept there.

What you see Fix Canvas shows its own error; Summit's log has a login and no launch after it The developer key's Redirect URIs must include https://ai2.unity.edu/summit/lti/launch, and the key must be On. issuer ... is not LTI_PLATFORM_ISSUER The key is in a test or beta instance; set LTI_PLATFORM_ISSUER. client id ... is not LTI_CLIENT_ID The key was recreated; copy the new client id. deployment ... is not in LTI_DEPLOYMENT_IDS Add the new install's deployment id, or empty the setting. login state unknown, expired or already used The launch took over 10 minutes or the page was reloaded mid-launch. Open the assignment again. "Summit learning is not configured on this server" A required secret is missing; Ready for Canvas? names it. A blank frame in Canvas Canvas is on a custom domain; set LTI_FRAME_ANCESTORS. "Choose a package" when opening the assignment The assignment was made without the picker. Edit it, choose External Tool, find Summit learning again and pick the course. Score missing from the gradebook Grades that didn't reach Canvas on the Canvas tab shows Canvas's answer. Fix the cause and select Resend.

docs.title: Before real students
docs.text:
These are FERPA education records. Before a live course uses this:

  • Get the registrar's sign-off on the data design (see SCORM courses and Canvas LTI).
  • Set up a backup with restricted access for the summit-learning-data volume. It is deliberately not in Summit's normal backups.
  • Decide on retention.

docs.title: SCORM courses and the Canvas LTI tool
docs.text:
Summit can host Articulate Storyline courses (SCORM 1.2, SCORM 2004 or xAPI packages) and play them inside Canvas through its own LTI 1.3 tool. Canvas handles the roster and the gradebook. Summit keeps every answer, the time on each slide and question, every click, and a timeline of everything the course reported, under a pseudonym, in a database of its own. It shows all of it under Learning in the sidebar, as a section of its own.

The feature is off until LEARNING_DATABASE_URL is set. Nothing changes for an instance that doesn't set it.

docs.title: How a launch works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Student in Canvas
    participant C as Canvas
    participant T as Summit LTI tool
    participant P as Summit player
    participant DB as Learning database
    S->>C: Opens the assignment
    C->>T: OIDC login (/lti/login)
    T->>C: Redirect to Canvas authorize, with state and nonce
    C->>T: Signed id_token (/lti/launch)
    T->>DB: Placement, pseudonymous learner, attempt, launch
    T->>P: 303 to /learn/play?t=attempt token
    P->>P: scorm-again runtime, course in an iframe
    P->>DB: Commits (/api/learn/commit) and call trace (/api/learn/trace)
    T->>C: Score to the gradebook (AGS) when the attempt is finished
  • Placing a course: an instructor adds an assignment with submission type External Tool and picks Summit learning. Canvas opens Summit's package picker (LTI Deep Linking), and the choice is stored on the assignment as a custom package_id.
  • Playing it: the player page exposes the SCORM API on its window (API_1484_11 for 2004, API for 1.2) and loads the course from /learn/content/<token>/... on the same origin, so Storyline finds the API the usual way.
  • Authorisation: no cookies are used inside Canvas's iframe. The launch mints a short-lived attempt token (2 hours by default, renewed while the course is open). Commits and traces carry it, and course files carry a separate content token in their path. The dashboard API key never reaches the browser.
  • Resume: each commit stores the whole CMI tree. The next launch hands it back with cmi.entry set to resume when the course exited with suspend, so Storyline's resume prompt works.
  • xAPI courses: Summit is the course's record store (LRS). The player opens the course with endpoint, auth, actor, registration and activity_id in the query string, the way Storyline and Rise expect, and the course sends its statements and resume state to /api/learn/xapi/ (xAPI 1.0.3: statements, state and profile documents). The auth is the attempt token, and the actor is the learner's pseudonym, so a course can only write to its own attempt.
  • Grades: when an attempt is completed, passed or failed, Summit posts the score (0 to 100) to the assignment's line item. A score is sent again only when it changes. A failure is shown on the attempt page and retried on the next commit. Instructor test launches are never graded.

docs.title: What is stored, and where
docs.text:
Everything lives in the learning database, not Summit's analytics database. It is not in the summit-backup dumps or in Summit's data export.

Table Holds packages Uploaded courses; files live under LEARNING_PACKAGES_DIR placements Canvas assignment or link, course title, line item learners One row per person: HMAC-SHA256(LEARNING_PSEUDONYM_KEY, iss + sub) learner_vault The Canvas user id, AES-256-GCM sealed with LEARNING_VAULT_KEY; only read to send a grade attempts, attempt_launches Status, score, total time, each sitting cmi_state The latest CMI tree for resume interactions One row per answer: response, correct answer, result, latency, timestamps; for Storyline quizzes also the quiz, its take and the try at that question (source = 'player'). Reports read the answer_rows view. runtime_calls Every SetValue, Commit, Initialize, Terminate with a browser timestamp (a Timescale hypertable) xapi_statements, xapi_documents Every xAPI statement as sent, and the state and profile documents (resume) learning_events One timeline for every kind of course: slides with time on each, clicks (with position and label), answers, typing (length only), media, tab switches, status and score audit_log Who viewed or changed learning data lti_launch_log Each Canvas login and launch: step, result, reason, course and assignment titles. No user ids. Kept 90 days.

The tool asks Canvas for anonymous privacy, so Canvas sends no names or email addresses. Learners show in the dashboard as the first 12 characters of their pseudonym. Typed free-text answers (fill-in, long-fill-in) are stored as [free text not stored] unless LEARNING_CAPTURE_FREE_TEXT=1.

These are still education records under FERPA, because the vault and the pseudonym key can link them back to a student. Treat the learning database, its backups and the three keys accordingly, and check retention and access with the registrar before real students use it.

docs.title: What the analytics show
docs.text:
The page watcher in the player sees the course page directly (it is served from Summit's own origin): which Storyline slide is showing, what the learner clicks and where, how much they type (never what), media play and pause, and when they leave the tab. SCORM calls and xAPI statements add answers, status and score. All of it lands in learning_events.

Storyline quizzes are read from the page too. A Storyline course reports its answers and score to the LMS only when its tracking is tied to a quiz result slide. Courses published to "track using completion trigger" send nothing about the quiz, so SCORM alone shows no answers. The watcher listens to Storyline's own quiz events (interaction:evaluated on every submit, quiz:completed when a take is finished), which fire whatever the tracking setting is. Each submit is stored with the text of the choice the learner picked (read from the slide, not Storyline's "Choice A"), the correct answer, right or wrong, which try at that question it was, and which take of the quiz. Each finished take stores its score, percent and pass or fail. When a course sends its own answers as well, the player's copy is the one reports use, so nothing is counted twice. Free-text answers are never sent from the page, only their length.

  • Overview: learners, attempts, answers, slide views, clicks, median time, 30 days of activity, and a card per course.
  • Course page: completion and pass rates; a slide funnel (how many attempts reached each slide, median and average time, where unfinished attempts stopped); a card per question with the share of each answer, correct rate, right-first-try rate and median time to answer; a click map per slide and the most clicked objects; each learner's progress, answers and quiz takes. CSV exports of every event and every answer.
  • Attempt page: time on each slide, each quiz take (right first try, wrong submits, result), every submit next to the correct answer with its try and take, the click map, the full timeline, and the raw SCORM calls or xAPI statements.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Variable Needed Meaning LEARNING_DATABASE_URL yes The separate learning database. Unset turns the feature off. LEARNING_PSEUDONYM_KEY yes 32 bytes, base64 or hex. Changing it gives every learner a new pseudonym. LEARNING_VAULT_KEY yes 32 bytes. Losing it means grades can't be sent for existing learners. LEARNING_TOKEN_SECRET yes 32 bytes. Signs attempt, content and deep-link tokens. SUMMIT_PUBLIC_URL yes Public https URL including the basePath, such as https://example.edu/summit. LTI_CLIENT_ID yes The Canvas developer key's client id. LTI_TOOL_PRIVATE_KEY yes RSA private key (PEM, \n escapes allowed). Its public half is served at /lti/jwks. LTI_PLATFORM_ISSUER no https://canvas.instructure.com (default). Test and beta instances use https://canvas.test.instructure.com and https://canvas.beta.instructure.com. LTI_DEPLOYMENT_IDS no Comma-separated deployment ids to accept. Empty accepts any deployment of the client id. LTI_AUTH_LOGIN_URL, LTI_AUTH_TOKEN_URL, LTI_JWKS_URL no Follow the issuer: sso.canvaslms.com for production, sso.test.canvaslms.com or sso.beta.canvaslms.com for the test and beta instances. Set them only for a self-hosted Canvas. LTI_TOKEN_AUDIENCE no aud of the grade-token request. Defaults to the token URL. LTI_TOOL_KEY_ID no kid of the tool key, summit-1 by default. LTI_FRAME_ANCESTORS no Who may frame the player. Default 'self' https://*.instructure.com https://*.canvaslms.com. LEARNING_PACKAGES_DIR no Where unpacked courses live. /data/learning-packages in compose. LEARNING_MAX_PACKAGE_MB no Upload limit, 1024 by default. LEARNING_ATTEMPT_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS, LEARNING_CONTENT_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS no Token lifetimes, 2 hours and 12 hours. LEARNING_CAPTURE_FREE_TEXT no 1 keeps typed answers. LEARNING_ALLOW_COURSE_CONNECTIONS no 1 lets course pages connect to other sites. Off, they can only reach Summit, which also blocks Storyline's own telemetry to metrics.articulate.com. LEARNING_DEMO_MODE no 1 turns on Try a course: play any course as a made-up demo learner without Canvas. For local demos only.

Generate the keys once per environment:

cd dashboard && npm run learning:keys

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. Start the learning database. With compose, set LEARNING_DB_PASSWORD and LEARNING_DATABASE_URL in .env, then run docker compose --profile learning up -d. It has its own volume and is not mounted into the backup sidecar. The production deploy script runs plain docker compose up -d --build, so there set COMPOSE_PROFILES=learning alongside the other secrets (Infisical, /summit) and the profile is picked up.
  2. Set the keys and URLs above in .env. The dashboard container applies the learning migrations on start (npm run migrate:learning does the same by hand).
  3. Give people access. Admins can see learning data. Anyone else needs Settings, Accounts, Allow learning data.
  4. Create the Canvas developer key (Canvas admin): Admin, Developer Keys, Developer Key, LTI Key. Choose Enter URL and paste SUMMIT_PUBLIC_URL/lti/config. Set the redirect URI to SUMMIT_PUBLIC_URL/lti/launch. Save it, switch it on and copy the client id into LTI_CLIENT_ID.
  5. Install the app in a sub-account or course: Settings, Apps, View App Configurations, + App, By Client ID. Copy the deployment id into LTI_DEPLOYMENT_IDS if you want to restrict it.
  6. Upload a course. In Storyline, publish for LMS as SCORM 2004 (3rd or 4th edition) and upload the zip under Learning in the Summit sidebar.
  7. Place it. In Canvas, create an assignment, set the submission type to External Tool, find Summit learning and pick the course. Set the points.

Learning, Canvas in the dashboard checks each of these settings, lists the values to hand the Canvas admin, and has a Check the connection to Canvas button. It fetches Canvas's signing keys, fetches Summit's own key set through the public address, and asks Canvas for a grade token. That token only comes back once the developer key is on and points at this server, so a pass there means launches and grades will work.

docs.title: Testing in a dev course
docs.text:
For the full walkthrough, including every Infisical secret, see Setting up the Canvas LTI tool.

A sandbox course in the real Canvas is the usual place: it uses the production issuer, and Student View gives a test student whose grades go to the gradebook like anyone's.

  1. Deploy Summit with Learning on (the settings above), reachable over https from the internet. If the reverse proxy limits request size, raise it for /summit/api/learning/packages so course zips can be uploaded (nginx: client_max_body_size 1024m).
  2. Open Learning, Canvas. Fix anything marked Fix, except the client id.
  3. Ask the Canvas admin for a developer key. Send them the JSON URL and Redirect URI from that page. They create it with Enter URL, switch it on and send back the client id. Put it in LTI_CLIENT_ID and redeploy.
  4. Check the connection to Canvas. All three should pass.
  5. Install it in the dev course: Settings, Apps, View App Configurations,
  6. App, By Client ID. Course admins or teachers can do this if the account allows it; otherwise the admin installs it in a sub-account.
  7. Upload a course and place it (Courses tab, then a Canvas assignment with External Tool and Summit learning).
  8. Play it as a student. Use Student View, or a test account enrolled as a student. The launch appears under Recent launches, the attempt under the course's analytics, and the score in the Canvas gradebook. Launches by teachers and designers are kept but marked instructor: they get no grade and stay out of the statistics.

When a launch fails, Recent launches on the Canvas tab says which step and why, without user ids. Common first-launch problems:

What you see Cause A login with no launch after it The developer key's Redirect URIs don't include SUMMIT_PUBLIC_URL/lti/launch, or the key is off. Canvas shows its own error and never posts back. issuer ... is not LTI_PLATFORM_ISSUER A test or beta Canvas instance; set LTI_PLATFORM_ISSUER to match. client id ... is not LTI_CLIENT_ID The key was recreated; copy the new client id. deployment ... is not in LTI_DEPLOYMENT_IDS Installed somewhere new; add the id or empty the setting. login state unknown, expired or already used The launch took over 10 minutes, or a page was reloaded mid-launch. Open the assignment again. The tool's page refuses to show inside Canvas Canvas on its own domain; add it to LTI_FRAME_ANCESTORS. Grades listed under Grades that didn't reach Canvas Canvas's answer is shown beside each. Fix the cause and select Resend.

docs.title: Demo on your own machine
docs.text:
tools/learning-demo runs Summit with Learning and demo mode on, in Docker, with its own two databases. Put course zips in tools/learning-demo/packages/ and run:

tools/learning-demo/run.sh

It prints the address (http://localhost:3300/summit/dashboard/learning) and a generated admin password. Try a course plays a course as demo learner A, B or C, with what Summit records shown live beside it. See tools/learning-demo/README.md, including sharing it on your tailnet with tailscale serve.

docs.title: Try it locally
docs.text:
tools/learning-e2e runs the whole flow against a fake Canvas: upload, deep linking, a learner launch, a real headless Chromium answering the sample quiz, the database contents, the score Canvas receives, resume on relaunch and the dashboard pages.

# A local TimescaleDB, user and password summit, on port 5432
docker run -d --name summit-learning-test -p 5432:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=summit -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=summit -e POSTGRES_DB=summit \
  timescale/timescaledb:latest-pg16
psql postgres://summit:summit@localhost:5432/summit -c "CREATE DATABASE summit_main_e2e" -c "CREATE DATABASE summit_learning_e2e"

cd dashboard && npm ci && npm run build
DATABASE_URL=postgres://summit:summit@localhost:5432/summit_main_e2e npm run migrate
LEARNING_DATABASE_URL=postgres://summit:summit@localhost:5432/summit_learning_e2e npm run migrate:learning

cd ../tools/learning-e2e && npm install
npx playwright install chromium   # on macOS; Linux uses the bundled build
npm run setup             # throwaway keys and server env
npm run canvas &          # fake Canvas on :3199
npm run server &          # Summit on :3100
npm test

docs.title: Limits and open questions
docs.text:
• One SCO per package. Storyline publishes one, which is the common case. Multi-SCO packages play only their first launchable item, and SCORM 2004 sequencing is not implemented.
  • cmi5 packages are refused. xAPI (Tin Can) packages play against Summit's own record store; cmi5's launch and session rules aren't done.
  • xAPI answers depend on the course. Storyline sends an answered statement per question with the response and result; Summit reads those. Other tools' statements are kept whole, but may need mapping to show as answers.
  • Slides are read from Storyline's player. Other tools still get clicks, typing, media and tab switches, but their slides come only from what the course reports.
  • Login state is checked on the server only. It is single use and expires in 10 minutes, but it is not tied to the browser with a cookie, because cookies are unreliable in Canvas's iframe. The LTI platform storage (postMessage) flow would close this; it's a follow-up.
  • Tokens ride in URLs. The commit beacon sent on page close can't carry headers, so the attempt token is in the query string. Pages send Referrer-Policy: no-referrer (same-origin for course files), and tokens are short-lived, but they can appear in reverse-proxy access logs. Consider stripping query strings from those logs.
  • Course files are served by Next.js. That is fine for typical courses. For large video, serve LEARNING_PACKAGES_DIR from the reverse proxy instead.
  • Not yet tried against a real Canvas. The flow follows Canvas's LTI 1.3 documentation and passes the local run above, but the first real launch is where surprises show up. The Canvas tab's launch log is there to catch them.
  • Analytics are per course package, not per Canvas course. If the same package is placed in a dev course and a real one, their learners are counted together. The Canvas tab shows each assignment's own counts.

docs.title: Connect a Unity game to Summit
docs.text: Install SummitAnalytics.cs on a persistent GameObject. Set apiUrl to the Summit origin and apiKey to the game's app key. SummitAnalytics supplies the /summit path itself. Test the network flow in a player build because analytics uploads are disabled in the Unity Editor.

docs.title: Instrument a session
docs.text:
Use a stable pseudonymous player ID. Call Identify before you start a session or queue that player's first event.

analytics.Identify(playerId);
analytics.StartSession(appVersion: Application.version);
analytics.Track("checkpoint_reached", numericValue: 1f);

Use the same event name for every occurrence of the same action. Put the level, checkpoint, or other changing context in properties. Put named numeric values, such as elapsed seconds, in properties.measurements. Send durable device details with SendHardwareProfile(). Call EndSession() where your game marks the end of the play session.

docs.title: Link a Trailhead replay
docs.text:
Subscribe to OnSessionStarted before you call StartSession. Pass the received ID and the same player ID to Trailhead's LinkSummitSession.

sequenceDiagram
    participant G as Unity game
    participant S as Summit
    participant T as Trailhead
    G->>S: Start a session with the player ID
    S-->>G: Return the session UUID
    Note over G: OnSessionStarted links the recorder
    G->>T: Upload recording with Summit session UUID
    T-->>G: Accept the recording
    T->>S: Sync recording summary and replay URL
    Note over S,T: Opening replay loads the frames in Trailhead

The recorder can start while Summit is still opening the session. OnSessionStarted runs when Summit issues an ID, including after a successful retry. Check for summit_session_id on the saved recording if it appears in Trailhead but is missing from the Summit session.

For the full SDK, including the Virtual Forest handshake and player feedback components, use the Unity client guide.

docs.title: Trailhead
docs.text:
Trailhead records the motion and events of a Unity session and replays them in a browser. Use it to see where a player moved, what a tracked object was doing, and which events occurred around a point in the recording.

Replay the bundled sample to try the viewer. Record from Unity to instrument a scene, or see the recording and sync reference for upload and storage details.

docs.title: From a Unity scene to the replay viewer
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Game["Unity game"] -->|Whole recording or segments| API["Trailhead ingest"]
    API -->|Recording JSON| Files[("Recording volume")]
    API -->|Metadata and status| DB[("PostgreSQL")]
    DB -->|Recording listing| Viewer["Trailhead dashboard"]
    Files -->|Frames and events| Viewer
    API -->|Optional recording summary| Summit["Summit"]
    Summit -->|Replay link| Viewer

The dashboard reads metadata from PostgreSQL and loads the recording JSON from disk for playback. A summary in Summit can link back to that replay.

docs.title: Source map
docs.text: Area Location Unity recorder Client example and API guide Replay controls and view Viewer components Payload structure Recording types Database setup SQL migrations

docs.title: Replay a sample recording
docs.text: Use the repository's sample recording to check ingestion, storage, and the 3D viewer together. The sample has positions and events you can inspect as soon as the upload finishes.

docs.title: Start Trailhead
docs.text:
1. From the repository root, copy .env.example to .env.
  2. Set DB_PASSWORD and API_KEY to local test values.
  3. Run docker compose up --build -d.
  4. Open the recordings gallery.

Compose starts PostgreSQL, applies the Trailhead migrations on application startup, and mounts a volume for recording files.

docs.title: Upload the fixture
docs.text:
Set API_KEY in your shell to the value from the local .env file. Run the command from the repository root.

base=http://localhost:8087/trailhead

curl --fail-with-body -sS "$base/api/recordings" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-api-key: $API_KEY" \
  --data-binary @fixtures/sample-recording.json

The response contains the new recording's id. Open http://localhost:8087/trailhead/recording?id=<id> with that value.

Press Play and scrub backward to an earlier moment. Use the subject panel to see what Trailhead tracked, and use the events panel to inspect a timestamp. Reload the gallery to see the saved recording.

If the request returns 401, check that the key in the shell matches the one the container received. Check the /trailhead prefix if the request returns 404. Trailhead uses that prefix for both development and production builds.

docs.title: Ingest routes
docs.text:
Trailhead uses the /trailhead base path. Both upload routes take the Trailhead API_KEY in x-api-key and accept JSON or gzip-compressed JSON with Content-Encoding: gzip.

Mode Route after the base path Recording ID State Whole recording POST /api/recordings Trailhead assigns it and returns it with 201 Finalized on acceptance Incremental POST /api/recordings/{id}/segments The client chooses a UUID before the first request Playable after upload, finalized by a segment with final: true Replay GET /recording?id={id} The same ID used by the gallery and Summit link Loads the saved frames and events

The default body ceilings are 16 MiB for a whole recording and 2 MiB per segment. Trailhead applies limits to the decoded JSON as well. The whole-file route returns 422 if its recorded duration is under 20 seconds or its recorded move count is zero, when those values are supplied. The incremental route can report discarded: true for those conditions on finalization.

docs.title: Incremental recordings
docs.text:
Each segment has a stable segmentId for retries. Send only new frames and events, address subjects by index, and set isNew on a newly introduced subject. A retried segment reuses its original ID. The server also drops frames and events repeated by overlapping segments.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Recording: First segment
    Recording --> Recording: More accepted segments
    Recording --> Finalized: Accepted final segment
    Recording --> Discarded: Final segment fails duration or move filter

The first segment can also be the final segment. An interrupted client can leave a playable recording in progress. PostgreSQL tracks recording state and segment IDs, while the recording volume holds the JSON used in the viewer.

docs.title: Summit sync settings
docs.text:
Setting Purpose SUMMIT_API_URL Summit base URL, including /summit for the Docker or production build SUMMIT_APP_API_KEY Summit app key Trailhead uses to submit the summary TRAILHEAD_PUBLIC_URL Browser-facing Trailhead base URL, including /trailhead, used to construct replay links SUMMIT_SYNC_URL Optional full URL override for incremental upload syncs

Trailhead submits summaries after accepting a whole recording or a segment. The sync is best effort. A recording can play in Trailhead while its summary is missing from Summit. Check the Summit URL and key, and confirm that the recording's summit_session_id belongs to an existing Summit session.

docs.title: Record from Unity
docs.text: Add TrailheadRecorder.cs to a persistent GameObject. Configure apiUrl with the Trailhead base URL, including /trailhead. Set apiKey to the server's recording upload key. The example logs the payload size in the Editor. Run a player build to upload.

docs.title: Track the objects that explain a session
docs.text:
1. Call Identify(playerId) with a stable pseudonymous ID.
  2. Call StartRecording("Forest walkthrough").
  3. Call AddSubject("Player", playerCamera.transform) and save the returned index.
  4. Mark a meaningful moment with AddSubjectEvent(playerIndex, "Checkpoint reached").
  5. Call FinishRecording() when play ends.

The subject index identifies the tracked object, even if other subjects have the same name. Use AddEvent for events that apply to the entire recording and SetMetadata for context such as the game mode. Use ClearSubjects between sessions when each session registers its own objects.

Subscribe to OnUploadComplete before finishing the recording. If it returns an ID, open GetReplayUrl(id) in the browser. The example client sends one complete file. Clients that need to save progress during browser play can use the segmented upload route.

docs.title: Keep the Summit session attached
docs.text:
When Summit and Trailhead run in the same game, use the same player ID for both. Subscribe to Summit's OnSessionStarted before starting its session. Call Trailhead's LinkSummitSession(sessionId, playerId) with the ID from the callback. When the server syncs the recording summary, Summit can attach it to the original session.

See the Unity recorder guide for render metadata and a complete code example.

docs.title: Waste Management
docs.text:
SludgeTower is a Unity card game and tower defense simulation. Players place defenses and manage resources between waves. Issues move along waypoint paths toward the end of the board.

Open the interactive waypoint explainer to see how a path guides moving objects. Use Verify analytics and replay to trace the same board activity through Summit and Trailhead.

docs.title: How one placement becomes two records
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Place["Player places an object"] --> Capture["WasteBoardReplayRecorder"]
    Capture -->|Placement and measurements| SummitClient["SummitAnalytics"]
    Capture -->|Cell event and recorded subjects| TrailClient["TrailheadRecorder"]
    SummitClient --> Summit["Summit event timeline"]
    TrailClient --> Trailhead["Trailhead board replay"]
    Summit -->|Linked replay| Trailhead

WasteBoardReplayRecorder subscribes to board, phase, level, and issue events. The recorder gives Trailhead the board dimensions and transform so the viewer can reconstruct cell positions. It sends object activity to Summit as named events with properties and measurements. Trailhead records movement for tracked subjects, such as the player camera and moving issues.

docs.text: Area Source Turn and wave progression Core/TurnController.cs Board events and metadata Core/WasteBoardReplayRecorder.cs Incremental replay upload Core/TrailheadRecorder.cs Analytics queue Core/SummitAnalytics.cs

docs.title: Verify analytics and replay
docs.text:
Use a development build and test instances of Summit and Trailhead. On the Game Master in the Main scene, configure SummitAnalytics with the Summit origin and game app key. Configure TrailheadRecorder with the Trailhead URL including /trailhead and the Trailhead recording upload key. Leave WasteBoardReplayRecorder.startOnLaunch enabled for automatic capture.

  1. Start a session and place a defense. Play long enough to capture a meaningful board change and let the recorder send a segment.
  2. In Summit, open the game's session and find the placement on its timeline.
  3. Follow the replay link. Check that the board shows the placement at the corresponding point on the replay timeline.
  4. End the session and reopen the recording to check that the last activity appears.

If Trailhead shows the recording but Summit has no replay link, check that the recording carries the Summit-issued session UUID. Check Trailhead's server-side Summit sync settings if it has the UUID.

docs.title: What happens in a browser
docs.text:
The Waste Management recorder sends segments while the game is running. Its default interval is 15 seconds. A tab becoming hidden asks for a checkpoint. A page unload requests a final segment. Both browser callbacks are best effort. The last segment can be lost when the tab closes, and earlier accepted segments remain available to replay.

When testing that path, wait for a recording to appear in Trailhead before hiding or closing the tab. Use a separate session to check normal finalization.

docs.title: XR Tools
docs.text: XR Tools is a Tauri desktop app for the people who build and publish XR experiences. It can upload a web build over FTPS, generate commit and changelog drafts, and prepare a Gource visualization of a repository's history.

docs.title: Choose a tool
docs.text:
Task Tool Requirements Upload a web build FTP Deploy A local build, hosting credentials, and a destination Calculate biweekly pay dates Pay Dates The latest pay date and the number of years Draft a Plastic SCM commit message AI Commit cm on PATH and an OpenAI API key Visualize Git or Plastic SCM history Gource Logs git or cm on PATH, plus gource to play the visualization Draft a changelog from history Changelog A Git or Plastic SCM checkout and an OpenAI API key for AI drafts

Review the repository content selected for an AI draft before sending it. The AI commands can send commit messages, status output, or diff content to OpenAI. Review the generated text before you use it.

docs.title: How work leaves the desktop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    UI["Vite interface"] --> Rust["Tauri commands in Rust"]
    Rust --> FTP["FTPS hosting"]
    Rust --> VCS["Git or Plastic SCM"]
    Rust --> Gource["Gource log and playback"]
    Rust --> AI["OpenAI for selected AI commands"]

Start with a test deployment if you are delivering a web build. Use the development and release guide to work on the desktop app itself.

docs.title: Deploy a test build
docs.text:
Use FTP Deploy to publish an XR web build to a test destination. Start with a build folder that already runs locally.

  1. Open FTP Deploy in the desktop app.
  2. Choose the local build folder.
  3. Choose a destination in the test group.
  4. Enter the credentials for the destination.
  5. Select Upload build.
  6. After the upload finishes, open the test site and check that it loads the expected build and its assets.

The Rust backend validates the target and local build before uploading. It uploads into a staging folder and promotes that folder after the upload succeeds. When a previous build exists, the server keeps it during promotion so recovery can restore it if a rename fails.

If the upload fails during a rename, read the recovery paths in the app's error and confirm which build is live before retrying. If the TLS connection fails, check that the configured host matches the certificate. The app requires explicit FTPS with an encrypted data connection.

docs.title: Run the desktop app
docs.text:
Install Node.js, Rust, and the native prerequisites for Tauri on your platform. Run these commands from the repository root.

npm ci
npm run dev

Use npm run build to produce a desktop bundle. Use npm run web:dev for Vite-only interface work and the desktop window to exercise commands that call Rust.

Area Source Tool interface and update prompt src/main.js Native commands and VCS integration src-tauri/src/tools/ Installers and signed updater bundles Release workflow

docs.title: Verify a release
docs.text:
1. Run Release from the repository's Actions tab with the intended version.
  2. Check the GitHub release for the Linux, Windows, and macOS installers.
  3. Check the updater service for the Windows x86-64 and Apple Silicon bundles.
  4. Open an older compatible desktop build. On launch, check that it offers the new version, then install it and confirm the app reports the new version.

The workflow points the packaged app at the configured HTTPS updater service. The app verifies the downloaded update against its embedded public key. Keep the matching signing key available to the release workflow. See the repository setup instructions for local updater testing and GitHub secret names.

docs.title: XR Tools Updater Service
docs.text:
The updater service distributes signed XR Tools updates. Release CI sends a Tauri manifest and platform bundle. An installed app asks whether it has an update for its platform and current version.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as XR Tools release workflow
    participant U as Updater service
    participant V as Release volume
    participant A as Installed XR Tools app
    C->>U: Send manifest and signed bundle
    U->>V: Store artifacts and update latest manifest
    A->>U: Check with target, architecture, and version
    U-->>A: Return download URL and signature for a newer build
    A->>U: Download the bundle
    Note over A: Tauri verifies the signature before installation

The service rewrites the manifest's download URLs to point at its hosted artifacts. Uploads for the same version can add platform entries to the version's manifest. The app-level manifest determines which version clients see.

See Check an updater release for the API and a readiness check. For server setup, use the repository README.

docs.title: Read the manifest and check the platform
docs.text:
Set UPDATER_URL to the HTTPS service URL for a test environment. Check that the service responds, then inspect the manifest for the app.

curl --fail-with-body -sS "$UPDATER_URL/health"
curl --fail-with-body -sS "$UPDATER_URL/api/apps/xr-tools/static/latest.json"

If the environment requires client authentication, send the configured bearer token with the manifest, update-check, and download requests.

Choose a version lower than the manifest version. For example, if the manifest promotes a version above 3.0.0, check the Apple Silicon entry this way.

curl --fail-with-body -i "$UPDATER_URL/api/apps/xr-tools/check/darwin/aarch64/3.0.0"

Expect 200 with a version, download URL, and signature when a newer bundle exists for that platform. Repeat with the manifest version and expect 204. A newer version without a bundle for the requested platform returns 404. Confirm that each expected platform is present after release jobs finish.

docs.title: Service reference
docs.text:
Route Purpose GET /health Confirm the server can open its data directory POST /api/apps/{appId}/releases Accept a multipart manifest and its referenced files using the upload bearer token GET /api/apps/{appId}/static/latest.json Read the latest manifest across platforms GET /api/apps/{appId}/check/{target}/{arch}/{currentVersion} Get a newer bundle entry for one platform GET /download/{appId}/{version}/{asset} Download a stored release artifact

DATA_DIR is the persistent storage root. Set BASE_URL to the HTTPS origin that clients use to reach the service, so the manifest's download URLs resolve from the desktop app. UPLOAD_TOKEN authorizes release CI. The optional CLIENT_AUTH_TOKEN applies to manifest reads, update checks, and downloads.
